analysis.one_liner: Ends federal tax breaks, discounted royalties, and financing for oil, gas, and coal production.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal fossil fuel subsidies was referred to nine House committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the term ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would strip away decades of special tax treatment for oil, gas, and coal companies, including deductions and credits unique to the industry. It would raise the royalty rates companies pay to drill or mine on public land, lift caps on their liability for offshore oil spills, and block US export and development agencies from financing fossil fuel projects abroad. It would also repeal the fast-track mandate for the Mountain Valley Pipeline and redirect the higher coal excise tax to the fund that pays black lung benefits to sick miners.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently make up the difference when fossil fuel companies pay reduced royalties, claim industry-only tax deductions, or leave spill cleanup costs beyond legal liability caps. Communities living near drilling, mining, and pipeline operations also benefit from stricter liability and repealed fast-tracked permitting. Coal miners with black lung disease benefit from a higher excise tax dedicated to their benefit fund.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and communities near extraction sites

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal royalty rate companies pay for coal, oil, and gas leases on public land from 12.5 percent to 18.75 percent, and ends royalty relief for offshore deep-water and shallow-water drilling.

Terminates industry-specific tax provisions, including the enhanced oil recovery credit, percentage depletion for coal, expensing of intangible drilling costs, and the LIFO inventory accounting method for oil, gas, and coal companies.
Removes statutory caps on the liability of offshore facilities and pipeline operators for oil spill damages, and denies tax deductions for oil spill removal costs and damages.

Prohibits the Export-Import Bank, the Development Finance Corporation, and other US agencies from financing fossil fuel projects, and rescinds contributions to international institutions that support them.
Repeals the Fiscal Responsibility Act sections that fast-tracked the Mountain Valley Pipeline and curtailed environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act.
Increases the excise tax that funds the Black Lung Disability Trust Fund, which pays benefits to coal miners disabled by mining work, from $1.10 to $1.38 per ton.

analysis.who_pays: Oil, gas, and coal companies, which would lose billions in industry-only tax deductions and credits and pay higher royalties and excise taxes. Banks and large asset managers that finance fossil fuel projects would lose their shield from cleanup liability, and companies shipping oil by pipeline would face uncapped liability for spills. Some of these higher costs could be passed through to consumers at the pump or on energy bills.

drawbacks.text: Companies facing higher royalties, excise taxes, and tax bills can pass some of the added cost through to consumers in the form of higher fuel and energy prices.

The bill terminates the carbon oxide sequestration credit entirely and restricts the clean hydrogen credit to renewable-powered production, cutting off tax support some see as necessary bridges for decarbonizing heavy industry.

The higher black lung excise tax and the loss of fossil fuel loan guarantees through the Rural Utility Service fall on coal-dependent firms and communities, where job losses would land on the same working people the bill's environmental provisions aim to protect.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill removes subsidies that go to some of the most profitable companies in the country and shifts cleanup risk and royalty shortfalls away from taxpayers. The main honest trade-off is that some of the cost would reach consumers through energy prices, and coal-dependent towns could take a further economic hit. The design is sweeping and complex, and its outright termination of the carbon capture credit is contested even among supporters of climate action.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2024 and referred to nine different House committees, then to three subcommittees, but no committee ever reported it and the House never voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ilhan Omar introduced the bill on May 23, 2024, joined by 32 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans.

The Speaker sent it to nine committees at once, including Ways and Means, Natural Resources, and Energy and Commerce, a referral pattern that lets a bill's provisions sit in several committees without any one of them moving it.

Over the following seven months, the bill was referred to three subcommittees, most recently the Trade subcommittee in December 2024, but received no markup, no hearing on the record, and no floor vote.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal companies are better off, because the industry-only tax breaks, below-market royalty rates, spill liability caps, and federal export financing all remain in place. Banks that finance fossil fuel projects also keep their protection from cleanup liability.

for.name: Rep. Ilhan Omar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal fossil fuel subsidies and wrote it across tax, royalty, liability, and federal financing law.

for.name: 32 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican did.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee of primary referral, which took no further action on the bill after it was sent there.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority controlling committee agendas and floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote during the remaining seven months of the session.

sides.party_line_note: All 33 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans holding 224 of 440 House seats the bill never left committee.

industries.note: Would lose the enhanced oil recovery and marginal well credits, intangible drilling cost expensing, LIFO inventory accounting, and royalty relief, pay a higher 18.75 percent royalty on federal leases, a new 13 percent Gulf of Mexico severance tax, and face uncapped offshore spill liability. These tax breaks and discounted public-land royalties are costs the public otherwise absorbs.

Would lose percentage depletion and capital gains treatment for coal royalties, pay a higher federal royalty and a larger black lung excise tax, and see the Powder River Basin studied for higher royalty capture. The excise increase would fund benefits for sick miners at the companies' expense.

industries.industry: Banks and large asset managers financing fossil fuels
industries.note: Would strip the CERCLA cleanup-liability shield from banks with $10 billion or more in assets and investment firms with $250 billion or more under management when they lend to polluting projects, and bar federal export and development agencies from financing fossil fuel projects.

Would lose the statutory $75 million-plus spill liability cap for offshore facilities, face full liability for onshore pipelines carrying tar-sands oil, and see the Mountain Valley Pipeline permitting fast-track repealed.
